title: Probiotics and Alcohol: Does Drinking Kill Probiotics?
excerpt: Can you drink while taking probiotics? What alcohol really does to probiotic bacteria and your gut, when to take them, the antibiotic question, and who should be careful.
metaDescription: Does alcohol kill probiotics? What drinking does to probiotic bacteria and your gut, when to take them, antibiotics, and who should be careful.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, you can generally drink alcohol while taking probiotics. There is no known dangerous interaction between the two for healthy adults, and a normal drink is unlikely to "kill" the bacteria in your capsule or yogurt before they reach your gut. The real tension is different: alcohol, especially heavy or frequent drinking, pushes your gut in the opposite direction from the one you're taking probiotics for. A probiotic can't cancel out a weekend of binge drinking. This guide explains what alcohol actually does to probiotic bacteria and to your own gut bacteria, whether timing matters, what the research does and doesn't show, and who should be careful.

**The quick rules:** Take your probiotic at a different time from drinking if you can, ideally with a meal the morning before or after. Don't expect a probiotic to prevent a hangover or protect your liver; there is no good evidence that it does. If you're taking probiotics alongside antibiotics, follow your prescriber's advice on alcohol for the antibiotic, which matters more than the probiotic. And if you have a weakened immune system, a serious illness, pancreatitis, or a central IV line, talk to your doctor before taking probiotics at all.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before taking probiotics if** you have a weakened immune system (from chemotherapy, an organ transplant, HIV, or long-term steroid use), you're seriously ill or recently hospitalized, you have a central venous catheter, you've had pancreatitis, you have short bowel syndrome, or you have liver disease. **See a doctor promptly if** you have bloody or black stools, severe or persistent belly pain, diarrhea lasting more than a couple of days, vomiting that won't stop, or fever along with gut symptoms after drinking. In an emergency, call 911.

## How Alcohol and Probiotics Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

There are two separate questions people mix together, and it helps to pull them apart.

1. **Does alcohol kill the probiotic bacteria you swallow?** This is about the bacteria in the pill, powder, or yogurt on their trip through your stomach and small intestine.
2. **Does alcohol undo what probiotics are supposed to do?** This is about your own gut bacteria (your microbiome) and your gut lining, which alcohol affects in ways that run against the goals of most probiotic use.

The first worry is mostly overblown. The second one is real, and it scales with how much you drink.

### Alcohol is an antiseptic, but only at high strength

Alcohol does kill bacteria. That's why hand sanitizer works. But hand sanitizer is usually 60 to 95 percent alcohol, and it relies on that high concentration to break bacterial cell walls quickly. Drinks are far weaker. Beer is typically around 4 to 6 percent alcohol, wine around 12 to 15 percent, and spirits around 40 percent. Once a drink hits your stomach, it mixes with stomach fluid and any food you've eaten, which dilutes it further.

The bacteria used in most probiotics, mainly **Lactobacillus** (many species have been renamed, for example to Lacticaseibacillus or Lactiplantibacillus) and **Bifidobacterium**, belong to the broad group called lactic acid bacteria. Some members of this group are tough enough to live in wine and beer. Winemakers deliberately use lactic acid bacteria to soften wine after fermentation, and brewers fight certain Lactobacillus strains that can spoil finished beer. That doesn't prove that every probiotic strain survives a cocktail, and tolerance varies a lot from strain to strain. But it does show that drink-strength alcohol is not the instant bacteria-killer people imagine.

### Stomach acid is the bigger hurdle

The harshest thing a probiotic faces on the way down is not alcohol. It's stomach acid, which is strong enough to kill many bacteria. Manufacturers deal with this by choosing strains that tolerate acid and bile, using capsules designed to release later in the gut, or recommending you take the product with food, which buffers stomach acid. Alcohol doesn't change that picture much. If anything, the practical advice to take probiotics with a meal does more for survival than avoiding a drink.

### Where alcohol really works against probiotics

The more meaningful conflict is what alcohol does to the environment probiotics are trying to support:

- **It shifts your gut bacteria.** Research in people who drink heavily over long periods has repeatedly found changes in the gut microbiome, often called dysbiosis. That usually means fewer of the bacteria associated with a healthy gut and more of the types linked to inflammation.
- **It loosens the gut lining.** Alcohol and its breakdown product, acetaldehyde, can weaken the tight seals between the cells lining your intestine. This is sometimes called increased intestinal permeability, or "leaky gut." When the seals loosen, fragments of bacteria (such as endotoxin, a molecule from the outer wall of certain bacteria) can slip into the bloodstream and stir up inflammation, including in the liver.
- **It irritates the stomach and speeds up the bowel.** That's part of why a big night can lead to an upset stomach or loose stools the next day.

A probiotic is meant to nudge things toward a balanced gut and a sturdy gut lining. Regular heavy drinking pushes the other way. Occasional moderate drinking is a much smaller push.

## Does Alcohol Kill Probiotics?

This is the question most people searching "probiotics and alcohol" actually want answered, so here it is plainly.

**For probiotic supplements:** there's little direct research testing whether a drink taken at the same time reduces how many probiotic bacteria survive in a person's gut. Based on how dilute drinks become in the stomach and how tough lactic acid bacteria tend to be, a normal drink is unlikely to wipe out a probiotic dose. Very strong drinks taken on an empty stomach right alongside your capsule are the scenario most likely to cause some loss, which is an easy reason to separate them.

**For probiotic foods:** yogurt, kefir, sauerkraut, and kimchi aren't harmed by you having a glass of wine with dinner. The alcohol is diluted in your stomach along with the food.

**For your own gut bacteria:** a single drink doesn't sterilize your gut. Your intestine holds trillions of bacteria, and moderate drinking doesn't kill them off in any meaningful way. The effects of alcohol on the microbiome are about gradual shifts in balance, mostly seen with heavy or long-term drinking, not a sudden die-off.

**What about alcohol killing bacteria in the bottle?** Some liquid probiotic drinks and tinctures contain a little alcohol as a preservative. Live-culture products don't use enough to sterilize themselves, and most probiotic supplements are dry capsules or powders anyway. Don't mix probiotic powder into a strong drink, though. There's no reason to, and it's the one setup where alcohol strength could matter.

## Can You Drink Alcohol While Taking Probiotics?

For most healthy adults, yes. There's no known harmful drug-style interaction, and probiotic labels don't carry an alcohol warning the way some medicines do. A few drinks while you're on a probiotic course won't make the probiotic dangerous.

What's fair to say is that drinking reduces the value you're getting from the probiotic. If you're taking one to settle your digestion, calm bloating, or recover from a stomach bug, alcohol is one of the things most likely to keep those symptoms going. The more you drink, the more you're working against the product you're paying for.

A sensible approach:

- **Keep drinking moderate** while you're trying to fix a gut problem. Fewer drinks, more slowly, with food.
- **Take the probiotic with a meal** at a time you're not drinking.
- **Notice patterns.** If your gut symptoms flare every time you drink, the alcohol is likely a bigger factor than the probiotic can offset. Our guides to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) and [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) cover what's normal and what isn't.

## When to Take Probiotics If You Drink

There's no study that establishes the best hour to take a probiotic around drinking, so be wary of anyone who gives you an exact schedule. What you can do is follow the general advice for probiotics and keep them apart from alcohol.

| Situation | Practical approach |
|---|---|
| You drink occasionally | Take your probiotic as usual, with a meal, on a schedule that doesn't line up with drinking. Morning with breakfast works for most people. |
| You're going out tonight | Take it with breakfast or lunch, not with your first drink. There's no evidence that taking extra beforehand helps. |
| The morning after | Take it with food once your stomach has settled. It won't fix the hangover, but there's no reason to skip your usual dose. |
| You're on antibiotics | Space the probiotic a few hours from the antibiotic dose (check with your pharmacist), and follow the antibiotic's alcohol advice. |
| You drink heavily most days | Talk to a doctor. A probiotic is not the fix here, and heavy drinking carries risks a supplement can't address. |

The label on your specific product may have its own instructions, such as taking it on an empty stomach or keeping it refrigerated. Follow those first.

## What the Research Actually Says

Most research on alcohol and the gut has been done in people who drink heavily or have alcohol-related liver disease, not in social drinkers. That matters, because results in those groups don't automatically apply to someone who has a few drinks on the weekend. With that caveat, here's where the evidence stands.

**Heavy drinking changes the microbiome and the gut barrier.** Studies in people with alcohol use disorder have found altered gut bacteria and signs of a leakier gut, and these changes have been linked to inflammation, liver injury, and even to mood symptoms such as depression and craving. A widely cited 2014 study in *PNAS* by Leclercq and colleagues found that a subgroup of alcohol-dependent patients had higher gut permeability and different gut bacteria, and that some of these changes improved after a few weeks without alcohol.

**Even a single binge can have short-term effects.** A 2014 study in *PLoS One* gave healthy volunteers a binge-level dose of alcohol and found a rise in bacterial endotoxin in the blood within hours. That's a sign that a heavy session can briefly let bacterial fragments past the gut barrier. It's a small study, and it doesn't show lasting harm from one night, but it fits the broader picture: dose matters.

**Probiotics in alcohol-related liver disease are an active research area.** Several small clinical studies, mostly in people already hospitalized or diagnosed with alcohol-related liver problems, have tested probiotics and reported improvements in some liver blood tests or markers of gut bacteria. Reviews generally describe these results as encouraging but limited by small sizes and short follow-up. They are not a reason for healthy people to take probiotics as liver protection before drinking, and they're certainly not a substitute for cutting back.

**Probiotics for hangovers have thin evidence.** Some products are sold as hangover probiotics, including engineered bacteria designed to break down acetaldehyde in the gut. There is no good evidence from large, independent human trials that probiotics reduce hangover symptoms in a meaningful way. We cover the products and claims in detail in our [hangover probiotics guide](/never-hungover/hangover-probiotics).

**Wine polyphenols are a separate story.** Some studies have found that red wine polyphenols (plant compounds also found in grapes and berries) can shift gut bacteria in ways researchers consider favorable. That's sometimes stretched into "wine is good for your gut." The more honest reading is that polyphenols may be helpful and you can get them from grapes, berries, tea, and dark chocolate without the alcohol.

For a deeper look at the gut science, see [how alcohol affects your gut microbiome](/never-hungover/how-alcohol-affects-your-gut-microbiome-the-hidden-health-impact-2025) and our guide to [protecting your gut health if you drink](/never-hungover/gut-health-alcohol-microbiome-protection).

## Probiotics, Antibiotics, and Alcohol

A lot of people start probiotics because they've been prescribed antibiotics, and then wonder about having a drink. There are really three things to keep straight.

- **The antibiotic is what matters for alcohol.** Most common antibiotics don't have a serious reaction with alcohol, but a few do. Metronidazole and tinidazole, for example, can cause flushing, nausea, vomiting, and a racing heart when combined with alcohol, and you're told to avoid alcohol during treatment and for a period afterward. Our guide to [antibiotics and alcohol](/never-hungover/antibiotics-and-alcohol) lists the main ones and what the labels say.
- **Probiotics with antibiotics have mixed but reasonable evidence.** Some reviews have found that certain probiotics can lower the chance of antibiotic-associated diarrhea in some groups. Results vary by strain and by person, so ask your pharmacist whether it's worth it for you.
- **Space the doses.** A common recommendation is to take the probiotic a couple of hours apart from the antibiotic, so the antibiotic doesn't kill the probiotic bacteria right away. Your pharmacist can give you a schedule that fits your specific antibiotic.

If you're sick enough to need antibiotics, your body is also busy fighting an infection, and alcohol can make you feel worse and sleep worse. Skipping it until you're better is usually the simplest choice.

## Fermented Drinks: Do Any Count as Probiotic?

Because beer, wine, and kombucha are all made by fermentation, people sometimes assume they're probiotic. Mostly they aren't.

- **Most beer and wine contain no meaningful live probiotics.** Commercial beer is usually filtered or pasteurized, and the yeast and bacteria used in winemaking are largely removed or inactive by the time you drink it. Some unfiltered, bottle-conditioned, or sour beers do contain live microbes, but they haven't been shown to deliver probiotic benefits, and the alcohol works against your gut anyway.
- **Kombucha and kefir can contain live cultures and a little alcohol.** Store-bought kombucha sold as non-alcoholic is generally kept under 0.5 percent alcohol in the US, while home-brewed kombucha can run higher. If you're avoiding alcohol completely, it's worth checking. Our guide on [how much alcohol is in kombucha](/never-hungover/how-much-alcohol-is-in-kombucha) has the details.
- **"Hard" kombucha is mainly an alcoholic drink.** Higher-alcohol versions are made to be drinks, not gut-health products. Treat them like beer.

If you want probiotic foods, yogurt with live cultures, kefir, sauerkraut, kimchi, and miso are better bets than anything with a meaningful alcohol content.

## Side Effects and Who Should Be Careful

For most healthy people, probiotics are well tolerated. The most common side effects are mild gas, bloating, or a change in bowel habits during the first week or two. Drinking can make those same symptoms worse, so if you start a probiotic and drink at the same time, it may be hard to tell which one is causing what.

Probiotics are live bacteria or yeasts, and in rare cases they can cause serious infections in vulnerable people. Talk to your doctor before taking them if you:

- **Have a weakened immune system**, for example from chemotherapy, an organ transplant, advanced HIV, or long-term high-dose steroids
- **Are critically ill, recently hospitalized, or have a central venous catheter** (a long-term IV line)
- **Have had pancreatitis.** This one matters for drinkers, because heavy drinking is a leading cause of pancreatitis. A Dutch trial published in *The Lancet* in 2008 gave a probiotic mix to patients with predicted severe acute pancreatitis and found more deaths in the probiotic group than in the placebo group. That result applies to severe hospital cases, not to healthy people, but it's a clear reason not to self-treat a pancreas problem with supplements.
- **Have liver disease or cirrhosis.** Probiotics are being studied in these conditions, and some doctors use them, but the decision belongs with your specialist.
- **Have short bowel syndrome or a damaged gut lining** from surgery or illness

Probiotic supplements are sold as dietary supplements in the US, so they aren't approved by the FDA for safety and effectiveness before sale the way medicines are. Products can vary in strain, dose, and how many live organisms actually remain by the expiration date. Choosing a brand that lists specific strains and a colony-forming unit (CFU) count guaranteed through the expiration date is a reasonable starting point.

## When to See a Doctor About Gut Symptoms After Drinking

Most gut trouble after a night out, such as an upset stomach, gas, or loose stools, settles within a day or so. A probiotic is not what you need if something more serious is going on. Get medical care if you notice:

- **Blood in your stool, black or tarry stools, or vomiting blood** (which can look like coffee grounds)
- **Severe belly pain**, especially pain in the upper belly that spreads to your back, which can be a sign of pancreatitis
- **Diarrhea that lasts more than two days**, or signs of dehydration such as very little urine, dizziness when standing, or confusion
- **Vomiting you can't stop**, or being unable to keep fluids down
- **Yellow skin or eyes**, dark urine, or swelling in your belly
- **Fever** along with gut symptoms

If your gut gets upset every time you drink, even with moderate amounts, it's worth mentioning to a doctor. Alcohol can unmask problems such as reflux, gastritis, irritable bowel syndrome, or food intolerances, and those have better treatments than guesswork.

## The Practical Takeaway: What Actually Helps Your Gut If You Drink

If you're taking probiotics because you care about your gut and you also drink, the biggest wins come from how you drink, not from the supplement:

- **Drink less per session.** The research on gut damage is overwhelmingly tied to heavy and frequent drinking. Fewer drinks per night does more than any capsule.
- **Eat before and while drinking.** Food slows alcohol absorption and is easier on your stomach lining. Our guide on [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) explains why.
- **Leave alcohol-free days in your week.** In the 2014 *PNAS* study, some gut changes in heavy drinkers improved after a few weeks of not drinking, a reminder that the gut can recover.
- **Feed your gut bacteria.** Fiber from vegetables, fruit, beans, oats, and whole grains feeds the bacteria you want. Probiotic foods like yogurt and kefir are fine additions.
- **Hydrate.** Alternate drinks with water, and have water before bed.
- **Keep the probiotic, if it helps you, but take it separately** from drinking, with a meal.

For a broader plan, see [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover), which focuses on the habits with the best evidence.

### Where DHM fits

Some readers who take probiotics also use DHM (dihydromyricetin), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, on nights they drink. It's a different tool with a different goal. DHM has been studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol and on the liver, mostly in animal and lab studies with a small amount of human data. It's promising, not proven, and there is no good evidence that it protects your gut microbiome or changes how probiotics work. There's also no known interaction between DHM and probiotics. If you'd like to try it, [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) are popular options. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. No supplement makes heavy drinking safe for your gut or your liver.

## The Bottom Line

- You can generally drink alcohol while taking probiotics. There's no known dangerous interaction for healthy adults.
- A normal drink is unlikely to kill the probiotic bacteria you swallow. Stomach acid is the bigger hurdle, and taking probiotics with a meal helps more than anything.
- The real conflict is that heavy or frequent drinking disrupts your gut bacteria and gut lining, which works against the reason you're taking probiotics.
- There's no good evidence that probiotics prevent hangovers or protect your liver from drinking.
- On antibiotics, the antibiotic's alcohol warning is what matters. Space probiotic doses from antibiotic doses as your pharmacist advises.
- If you have a weakened immune system, serious illness, a central line, pancreatitis, or liver disease, talk to your doctor before taking probiotics.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does alcohol kill probiotics?**

Not in any meaningful way at normal drinking levels. Alcohol kills bacteria at high concentrations, like the 60 to 95 percent found in hand sanitizer, but drinks are much weaker and get diluted further in your stomach. Many lactic acid bacteria, the group most probiotics come from, can tolerate drink-strength alcohol. To be safe, take your probiotic with a meal at a different time from drinking.

**Can I drink alcohol while taking probiotics?**

For most healthy adults, yes. There's no known harmful interaction, and probiotic products don't carry an alcohol warning. The catch is that heavy or frequent drinking disrupts gut bacteria and the gut lining, which works against the reason you're taking a probiotic. Keeping drinking moderate gives the probiotic a better chance to help.

**Should I take probiotics before or after drinking?**

There's no research showing a best time relative to drinking. A practical approach is to take your probiotic with a meal at a time you're not drinking, such as breakfast the morning before or after. There is no good evidence that taking extra probiotics before a night out reduces a hangover or protects your gut.

**Do probiotics help with hangovers?**

There is no good evidence from large, independent human trials that probiotics meaningfully reduce hangover symptoms. Some products marketed for hangovers use engineered bacteria meant to break down acetaldehyde, but the published human evidence is limited. Eating, hydrating, and drinking less remain the most reliable approaches.

**Can I drink alcohol while taking probiotics and antibiotics?**

The antibiotic decides that, not the probiotic. Most common antibiotics don't react badly with alcohol, but some, like metronidazole and tinidazole, can cause flushing, vomiting, and a racing heart and should not be combined with alcohol. Ask your pharmacist about your specific antibiotic, and space your probiotic a few hours away from the antibiotic dose.

**Is beer or kombucha probiotic?**

Most commercial beer and wine contain no meaningful live probiotics because they're filtered, pasteurized, or the microbes are inactive. Kombucha and kefir can contain live cultures, and non-alcoholic kombucha in the US is generally kept under 0.5 percent alcohol, though home brews can be higher. Yogurt, kefir, sauerkraut, and kimchi are better probiotic sources than any alcoholic drink.

**Can probiotics repair gut damage from alcohol?**

There's no good evidence that probiotics can undo gut damage from regular heavy drinking in healthy people. Small studies in people with alcohol-related liver disease have reported improvements in some markers, but those are early results in a specific group. The most effective way to help your gut recover is to drink less and give it alcohol-free days.

**Who should not take probiotics?**

Talk to a doctor first if you have a weakened immune system, are critically ill or recently hospitalized, have a central IV line, have had pancreatitis, have liver disease, or have short bowel syndrome. Probiotics are live organisms and can rarely cause serious infections in vulnerable people. A trial in severe acute pancreatitis found more deaths with probiotics, so don't self-treat a pancreas problem with supplements.
